questions.question: What is token authentication and when do you use it?
questions.title: Token Authentication
questions.direct_answer: Token auth is authenticating with a token the client sends on each request (usually in the Authorization header: Authorization: Bearer <token>), instead of a session cookie. It's used for APIs and SPAs where the client isn't a browser with cookies — mobile apps, other services, a React front end. On login the server issues a token (random, stored hashed in the DB, or a signed JWT), the client stores it and sends it on each request, and the server verifies it to find the user. It's stateless (no session to look up) and works cross-origin, unlike cookie sessions.

sections.title: Stateless Auth for APIs
sections.content: Token authentication is authenticating with a token the client sends on each request — usually in the Authorization header as Authorization: Bearer <token> — instead of a session cookie. It's used for APIs and SPAs where the client isn't a browser with cookies: mobile apps, other services, a React front end. On login the server issues a token (a random secret stored hashed in the database, or a signed JWT), the client stores it and sends it on each request, and the server verifies it to find the user. It's stateless (no session record to look up) and works cross-origin, unlike cookie sessions which are tied to a single domain.

sections.title: Login -> Token -> Each Request
sections.content:
The client logs in once, gets a token, and sends it on every request; the server verifies it.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  L[login] --> I[server issues token]
  I --> S[client stores token]
  R[each request] -->|Authorization: Bearer token| V[server verifies -> user]
```

sections.title: Token auth flow
sections.content:
```ruby
# Issue a token on login
class Api::SessionsController < ApplicationController
  def create
    user = User.authenticate(params[:email], params[:password])
    if user
      token = SecureRandom.hex(32)                # or a signed JWT
      user.update(auth_token: Digest::SHA256.hexdigest(token))  # store hashed!
      render json: { token: token }                # send to client
    else
      render json: { error: 'invalid' }, status: :unauthorized
    end
  end
end

# Verify on each request (a before_action)
class ApiController < ApplicationController
  before_action :authenticate_token!

  def authenticate_token!
    token = request.headers['Authorization']&.sub('Bearer ', '')
    user = User.find_by(auth_token: Digest::SHA256.hexdigest(token))
    render json: { error: 'unauthorized' }, status: :unauthorized unless user
    @current_user = user
  end
end
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Sending the token in a query param (logged in URLs) — use the Authorization header.
Storing tokens in localStorage (XSS can steal them); httpOnly cookie or memory is safer.
Storing the token in the DB in plaintext — store a hash, like a password.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Token auth: the client sends Authorization: Bearer <token> on each request.
Used for APIs/SPAs/mobile where the client isn't a browser with cookies.
Stateless — no session record to look up; works cross-origin.
On login the server issues a token (random+hashed in DB, or a signed JWT).
Store tokens hashed (like passwords); send in the Authorization header, not a query param.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: Token authentication is authenticating with a token the client sends on each request — usually in the Authorization header as Authorization Bearer token — instead of a session cookie. It's used for APIs and SPAs where the client isn't a browser with cookies: mobile apps, other services, a React front end. On login the server issues a token, a random secret stored hashed in the database or a signed JWT, the client stores it and sends it on each request, and the server verifies it to find the user. It's stateless, with no session record to look up, and works cross-origin, unlike cookie sessions which are tied to a single domain. A common mistake is sending the token in a query param, because that gets logged, instead of the Authorization header, or storing tokens in localStorage, where XSS can steal them, or storing the token in the database in plaintext, when you should store a hash like a password.
